strengths: Targets relation hallucination, a genuinely underexplored subtype (~40% of hallucinations) compared to the heavily studied object/attribute hallucination; the problem framing is relevant and well-motivated.

Proposes a training-free framework combining question decomposition (subject–object–relation masking), text-guided visual attention enhancement, and an interleaved text–image chain with attention-bias transfer; the multi-component design is reasonable and clearly described at a high level.

Evaluation spans two architectures (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP) and two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench), showing consistent (if modest) improvements over re-implemented relation-hallucination baselines.
Includes component-wise ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (k_max, lambda), qualitative case studies, and attention-map visualizations that support the claimed mechanism.
Practical: no training required, and inference overhead (~4x) is documented.
weaknesses: Modest gains: improvements over the best baseline are ~1.7% accuracy on MMRel and ~0.2–1.7% on R-Bench; no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across runs are reported, making it hard to assess whether the improvements are robust.

Limited and weak baselines: only two prior relation-hallucination methods (Constraint-Aware Prompting, Detect-then-Calibrate), both re-implemented. Missing comparisons to other plausible mitigations (e.g., generic CoT/self-consistency prompting, self-correcting decoding, retrospective resampling) and to modern LVLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL, LLaVA-1.6, GPT-4V-level models); the evaluated models are dated.

Potential confound between components: the ablations do not cleanly isolate the visual attention-bias mechanism from plain multi-step textual prompting (e.g., there is no baseline that uses the five decomposed questions with text-only context at full strength plus standard CoT prompting), so the source of the gains is not fully pinned down.

Technical underspecification: the confidence term Conf(prev_i) in Eq. 5 is never defined; how the attention bias is actually injected into which layers/heads of the LVLM decoder is only loosely described; Eq. 6's normalization is ad hoc. Reproducibility would be difficult without these details.

Narrow scope: the method assumes the question explicitly contains a subject, object, and relation and is Yes/No VQA; behavior on open-ended questions, captions, or questions where spaCy keyword extraction fails is not analyzed. Error propagation when early sub-answers (Q1/Q2) are wrong is neither measured nor mitigated.

Evaluation is limited to aggregate Yes/No accuracy/precision/F1; no per-relation-type breakdown (spatial/action/comparative) in the main results despite the authors acknowledging weaker spatial performance, and no failure-case analysis.

Presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('targted', 'contcext'), an inconsistency in Figure 2 ('[R]: stand' for a 'chase' example), a stale reference to 'Table 3a' for results shown in Figure 3a, and an inconsistent claim that a 'w/o Enhancement' ablation still outperforms baseline while other variants outperform it by larger margins—these suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Novelty is incremental: question decomposition, attention-based visual grounding, and interleaved multimodal CoT are each established; the contribution is primarily their composition for relation hallucination, and the improvement magnitude does not clearly establish the attention-transfer component as essential.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and meaningful problem: relation hallucinations in LVLMs, which the paper motivates with statistics (nearly 40% of hallucinations) and a clear taxonomy.
The method is training-free and model-agnostic, making it potentially applicable without retraining costs, and it is evaluated across two architecturally different LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP).

The paper includes a reasonable evaluation package: two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench), comparison with two targeted baselines, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (k_max and λ), and qualitative case studies with attention-map visualization.
Writing is generally organized and the pipeline (attention enhancement → question decomposition → interleaved chain) is described at a level that permits implementation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core ideas are largely combinations of well-known techniques: question decomposition/masking (standard CoT-style prompting), cross-attention with entity keywords (standard attention-guided grounding), and injecting attention-map biases into subsequent layers (similar to prior attention-modulation methods). The connection to ICoT (Gao et al., 2025) is acknowledged but the delta over ICoT and over simple multi-question prompting baselines is not clearly established.

Modest empirical gains. The improvement over the best baseline is only 1.7% accuracy on MMRel and 1.7% on R-Bench (76.04 vs 75.86 in accuracy for LLaVA), with no statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or per-category breakdowns. Given the added complexity, the evidence that ChainMPQ meaningfully outperforms strong prompting baselines is weak.

Restrictive problem setting. The method requires extracting a clean subject–object–relation triple from the question using spaCy and presumes Yes/No relational questions. This limits applicability to open-ended VQA, captioning, and questions where S/O/R extraction is ambiguous. Failure analysis for keyword-extraction errors is absent.

Evaluation is limited to two older 7B models (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP); no experiments with stronger recent models (e.g., Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL), and no evaluation on general benchmarks to check whether the method degrades standard VQA performance (potential regression from forced multi-step answering is not assessed).

Significant inference cost: the authors report ~4x inference time relative to the base model. Given the small accuracy gains, the cost–benefit trade-off is questionable and no efficiency comparison with baselines is provided.

Technical presentation issues: the confidence term Conf_previ in Eq. 5 is never formally defined; Eq. 6's normalization and accumulation of visual memory across rounds is underspecified; the distinction between visual memory V and enhanced tokens V′ in Algorithm 2 is confusing; several typos ('targted', 'contcext', 'texual', duplicate 'Q1' in Algorithm 2) suggest insufficient polish.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or incomplete: baselines were re-implemented by the authors, and other relevant training-free hallucination mitigation methods (e.g., VCD, M3ID, OPERA) are cited in the related work but not compared against on these benchmarks.

Attention-bias mechanism requires access to internal attention maps and cross-attention layers, which constrains portability to modern architectures (e.g., decoder-only models with different attention structure); only LLaVA-1.5-style and BLIP-2-style attention access is demonstrated.
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of released code or prompts; details such as how the five questions are verbalized for arbitrary relations and how answers are parsed into Yes/No are missing.

strengths: Targets an important and relatively underexplored problem: relation hallucinations account for a large fraction of LVLM errors, and the paper clearly motivates why single-step relational inference is prone to language-prior-driven errors.

The proposed framework is reasonable and well-motivated: subject-object-relation decomposition, multi-perspective question construction via systematic masking, and an interleaved chain that transfers both textual answers and visual attention memories across steps.

Training-free design makes the method plug-and-play and easy to combine with existing LVLMs; the paper reports results on two distinct architectures (LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP), which is a plus for generality claims.

Evaluation covers two relation-specific benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench) with standard accuracy/precision/F1, includes two tailored baselines (constraint-aware prompting, detect-then-calibrate), and provides ablations over all three proposed modules plus hyperparameter sensitivity analysis.

Case studies and attention map visualizations provide qualitative insight into how the chain reshapes the model's attention trajectory, and the appendix gives a detailed algorithm, implementation details, and dataset descriptions that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely an engineering combination of existing ideas (interleaved modal CoT from ICoT, question decomposition/masking, attention-bias steering similar to prior attention-mitigation work). The individual components are not fundamentally new, and the technical contribution is heuristic rather than principled.

Modest and weakly supported gains: improvements over the best baselines are small (~1.7 points on MMRel, ~1.8 on R-Bench). No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds is reported, so it is hard to judge whether the improvements are robust, especially given re-implemented baselines.

Narrow experimental coverage: only two 7B-generation models (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP) are evaluated. Stronger and more recent LVLMs (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, InternVL) are absent, leaving open whether the approach is relevant to modern architectures. Ablations are performed on only one model and one benchmark.

Potential evaluation confound not analyzed: the multi-perspective sub-questions and accumulated answers may leak/bias the final Yes/No decision (e.g., Q4 'Who is standing on the surfboard?' presupposes the relation). The paper does not control for this or measure whether gains come from genuine visual grounding vs. textual context steering. Also, no evaluation of whether the method degrades general VQA or object-level performance.

Technical clarity issues: Eq. (1)'s cross-attention formulation (visual features as Query, keyword embeddings as Key/Value) is simplistic and its integration into decoder-only architectures like LLaVA-1.5 is not clearly explained; the confidence term Conf_previ in Eq. (5) is never precisely defined; notation inconsistencies appear (e.g., Figure 2 labels [R] as 'stand' for a 'chase' example; typos such as 'contcext', 'targted').

Reliance on spaCy-based keyword extraction and fixed 5-question decomposition: failure modes when subject/object/relation extraction fails or questions are not canonical S-V-O forms are not analyzed, which limits claims of generality.

Practical cost is significant: inference time is ~4x the base model, and the cost-benefit trade-off versus the modest accuracy gains is not seriously discussed. No code release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility.

Figures 5 and 6 show attention maps for only cherry-picked examples; aggregate attention-based evidence or per-category results (the paper itself admits weaker performance on spatial relations) are missing.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem: relation hallucinations in LVLMs, which the authors motivate as ~40% of hallucinations, versus the heavy prior focus on object/attribute hallucinations.

The proposed method is training-free and model-agnostic, and is evaluated on four architecturally diverse LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5), supporting a generalization claim beyond a single model family.

Consistent improvements over the best baselines on two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel and R-Bench), with particularly notable precision gains, plus supplementary evidence on general benchmarks (MMBench, MME) in the appendix.

Reasonably thorough analysis: component-wise ablations (attention enhancement, multi-perspective prompts, interleaved chain), hyperparameter sensitivity (k_max, λ), latency/accuracy trade-off variants (Light1/Light2), attention map visualization, and qualitative case studies that illustrate the reasoning process.

The interleaved mechanism that transfers both textual context and attention-based visual memory across sub-questions is a sensible and non-trivial design choice distinguishing it from text-only prompting baselines.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is largely a combination of known ideas — question decomposition (S/O/R masking), interleaved multimodal CoT (explicitly building on ICoT, Gao et al. 2025), and attention-based visual token selection/biasing — packaged for relation hallucination. The technical contribution of Section 3.5 (top-k attention masks added as attention bias) is fairly standard.

The magnitude of improvement over the strongest baselines is modest (roughly 0.8–3.5% accuracy across settings), and no statistical significance testing, variance over seeds, or per-category breakdown on MMRel is reported in the main text.

The pipeline depends on spaCy for S/O/R extraction and GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement, which weakens the 'simple, robust' framing: errors in decomposition or question phrasing could propagate through the entire chain, and this failure mode is neither analyzed nor quantified.

Main evaluation is restricted to Yes/No VQA-style benchmarks; there is no evaluation on generative relation tasks (e.g., captioning with relation metrics), so the claim of 'improving relational inference in LVLMs' is narrower than suggested. The accuracy/F1 protocol on possibly imbalanced Yes/No data may not cleanly measure hallucination reduction.

Baseline coverage is thin for such a targeted area: only Constraint-Aware Prompting, Detect-then-Calibrate, and CoT, with other relation-hallucination approaches (e.g., dataset/scene-graph-based methods) mentioned in related work but not compared.

Several clarity and consistency issues: Typos ('contcext', 'targted'), an unexplained confidence term Conf_prev in Eq. 5 (its computation is never defined), apparent model-name inconsistency between Table 1 (InternVL3.5-8B) and appendix Table 3 (InternVL3-8B), and no statement of code/data release, which hurts reproducibility.

The evidence that 'improved relation reasoning leads to better general reasoning' (Appendix A.5) is correlational and lightly analyzed; gains on general benchmarks could stem from the extra reasoning turns rather than improved grounding.

strengths: Targets relation hallucination, a genuinely underexplored and significant problem (reported as ~40% of LVLM hallucinations), which gives the paper clear relevance to model reliability

Training-free, model-agnostic design evaluated across four architecturally distinct LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5) and two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench), demonstrating consistent gains

Reasonably thorough experimental analysis: component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity (kmax, lambda), an accuracy-latency trade-off study with Light variants, attention-map visualization, and general-benchmark evaluations (MMBench, MME) in the appendix
Case studies (Figure 4, 7) and the algorithmic description (Algorithm 1/2) make the pipeline fairly easy to follow end-to-end
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core recipe—decompose a question into subject/object/relation sub-questions, chain them with context, and bias attention toward attended tokens—combines well-established ideas (CoT, question decomposition, attention manipulation à la OPERA-style methods) with relatively little new conceptual insight; the delta over prior work (ICoT, Triplet Description, Constraint-Aware Prompting) is primarily an engineering combination

Narrow problem formulation: the method and evaluation are restricted to Yes/No relational VQA with cleanly extractable S-R-O triplets via spaCy; robustness to free-form questions, multiple relations, or compositional scenes is unexamined, and the failure mode when triplet extraction is wrong (cascading errors in intermediate answers) is not analyzed

Overhead is substantial (0.9s to 3.3s per sample, ~3.7x) and the gains are modest in several settings (e.g., InternVL3.5 on MMRel: 75.21 vs 74.45 for the Calibrate baseline, <1 point), raising questions about cost-effectiveness

Technical gaps in the method description: the confidence term Conf_prev in Eq. 5 is never defined (how is answer certainty measured?), Eq. 2's layer/attention aggregation is stated loosely, and adding a bias inside the softmax attention in this form is not well justified; why cross-attention with keywords as Key and Value (Eq. 1) yields 'enhanced' tokens is also under-explained

Hyperparameters (kmax=20, lambda=5) are tuned and sensitivity is analyzed only on LLaVA-1.5/MMRel, then applied everywhere; no statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for the main tables

Baseline coverage is thin: only two relation-hallucination-specific training-free baselines plus generic CoT; methods discussed in the introduction (e.g., Triplet Description Wu et al. 2025b, contrastive decoding, retrospective resampling) are cited as related but not compared, and a simple sub-question-only CoT ablation (text chain without the attention-bias machinery, at matched question count) is missing, making it hard to attribute gains to the visual-memory mechanism rather than just more questions

Writing quality issues (typos such as 'targted', 'contcext', duplicated panel content in Figure 4) and no mention of code release, which weakens reproducibility given the many implementation choices (GPT-3.5 question refinement, n=3 layers, entropy-based k selection)

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly scoped problem: relation hallucination is genuinely underexplored relative to object/attribute hallucination, and the paper positions its contribution against the existing taxonomy (Bai et al. 2024) and the ~40% prevalence statistic.

The proposed pipeline is reasonably well-structured into three interpretable modules (text-guided attention enhancement, multi-perspective question decomposition, interleaved text-image reasoning chain), and Algorithm 1/2 in the main text and appendix support reproducibility of the procedure.

Comprehensive evaluation for a training-free inference method: four architecturally distinct LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5) x two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench image-level), plus general-purpose benchmarks (MMBench, MME) in the appendix showing the method does not harm general ability.

Ablation study of all three core components (Table 3a) and sensitivity analysis of the two key hyperparameters (k_max, lambda) demonstrate that each module contributes and that the design choices are not arbitrary; consistent ablation trends support the paper's central claims.
The Light1/Light2 variants with an accuracy-vs-latency analysis (Table 2) are a practical addition, addressing the obvious 3.6x inference cost overhead of the full chain.
Qualitative case studies with per-step attention visualizations (Figures 4-7) provide intuitive mechanistic evidence consistent with the quantitative results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially question decomposition + CoT-style multi-turn prompting + attention-map-guided biasing, all well-established techniques (ICoT, POPE-style attention analysis, visual prompting). The integration is sensible but the individual ingredients and the overall recipe are incremental; the delta over existing relation-hallucination methods is modest (~1.7-2.6 points accuracy).

Small and potentially not robust gains: improvements over the strongest baselines are in the 0.7-2.6 point range, and no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, making it hard to judge whether some of the smaller margins (e.g., InternVL3.5 +0.76 over Calibrate) are meaningful.

The pipeline depends on GPT-3.5 Turbo for refining generated sub-questions (Appendix A.3), which weakens the 'training-free and self-contained' framing, adds hidden cost/variability, and raises reproducibility concerns (results may depend on a proprietary API's behavior).

Error-cascading risk is acknowledged only in Future Work but never analyzed: the final answer conditions on all five sub-answers, yet the paper provides no analysis or statistics on how often incorrect sub-answers propagate to incorrect final answers versus when the chain self-corrects.

Baseline coverage is thin: only two prior relation-hallucination mitigation methods (Constraint-Aware Prompting, Detect-then-Calibrate) plus vanilla CoT. Other relevant training-free approaches (e.g., visual prompting/contrastive decoding families, VCD, M3ID) are not compared, so the claimed superiority of the 'full text-image reasoning chain' is established against a narrow field.

Some technical components are under-specified or ad hoc: Eq. (1)'s cross-attention 'enhancement' (V as Query against keyword text as Key/Value) is unusual and its effect on how V' replaces visual tokens in the LLM is not clearly explained; the confidence-based weight alpha_i in Eq. (5) is described but its exact definition (how 'answer certainty' is computed) is never given; the w/o Interleaved ablation conflates removal of visual memory with a change in text-context length, making attribution imprecise.

Internal inconsistencies and polish issues: the model is referred to as InternVL3.5-8B in Section 4.1 but InternVL3-8B in Tables 3-4; there are typos in figures ('Multimodal contcext'), a duplicated/broken text block in Figure 7, and Wei et al. CoT is cited with both 2022 and 2023 dates. Figure 5's attention maps are too low-resolution to visually support the claims made about them.

Evaluation is restricted to binary Yes/No VQA formats on two benchmarks; there is no evaluation on open-ended relation description (e.g., triplet-level or caption-based metrics like Tri-HE), so the generality of the claim 'reduces relation hallucinations' beyond this specific question format is untested.
